arXiv:0711.3894v1 [math.AG] 25 Nov 2007

Plane Jacobian conjecture for simple polynomials

Nguyen Van Chau ††thanks: Supported in part by the National Basic Program on Natural Science, Vietnam, and ICTP, trieste, Italy. Affiliation: Institute of Mathematics, 18 Hoang Quoc Viet, 10307 Hanoi, Vietnam Affiliation: E-mail: nvchau@math.ac.vn
Abstract

A non-zero constant Jacobian polynomial map F=(P,Q):ℂ2⟶ℂ2F=(P,Q):\mathbb{C}^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}^{2} has a polynomial inverse if the component PP is a simple polynomial, i.e. if, when PP extended to a morphism p:X⟶ℙ1p:X\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} of a compactification XX of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}, the restriction of pp to each irreducible component CC of the compactification divisor D=X−ℂ2D=X-\mathbb{C}^{2} is either degree 00 or 11.

Keywords and Phrases: Jacobian conjecture, non-proper value set, rational polynomial, simple polynomial.

2000 Mathematical Subject Classification: 14R15.

1. Let F=(P,Q):ℂ2⟶ℂ2F=(P,Q):\mathbb{C}^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}^{2} be a polynomial map, P,Q∈ℂ⁡[x,y]P,Q\in\mathbb{C}[x,y], and denote J​F:=Px​Qy−Py​QxJF:=P_{x}Q_{y}-P_{y}Q_{x} the Jacobian of FF. The mysterious Jacobian conjecture (JC) (See [4] and [2]), posed first by Keller in 1939 and still open, asserts that FF has a polynomial inverse if the Jacobian J​FJF is a non-zero constant. In 1979 by an algebraic approach Razas [17] proved this conjecture for the most simple geometrical case when PP is a rational polynomial, i.e the generic fiber of PP is a punctured sphere, and all fibres P=cP=c, c∈ℂc\in\mathbb{C}, are irreducible. In attempt to understand the geometrical nature of (JC), this case was also reproved by Heitmann [5] and Lê and Weber [10] in some other approaches. In fact, as observed by Neumann and Norbudy in [12], every rational polynomial with all irreducible fibres is equivalent to the coordinate polynomial. Most recent, Lê in [7] and [8] present the following observation, which was announced in the Hanoi conference, 2006, and the Kyoto conference, 2007.

Theorem 1.

(Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.8 in [8]) A non-zero constant Jacobian polynomial map F=(P,Q)F=(P,Q) has a polynomial inverse if PP is a simple rational polynomial.

Here, following [11], a polynomial map P:ℂ2⟶ℂP:\mathbb{C}^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C} is simple if, when extended PP to a morphism p:X⟶ℙ1p:X\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} of a compactification XX of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}, the restriction of pp to each irreducible component ℓ\ell of the compactification divisor D=X−ℂ2D=X-\mathbb{C}^{2} is either of degree 00 or 11. In fact, as in the proof in [8] of Theorem 1, if a component of non-zero constant Jacobian map F=(P,Q)F=(P,Q) is a simple rational polynomial, then this component determines a locally trivial fibration.

In this short paper we would like to present an other explanation for Theorem 1 from view point of the geometry of the non-proper valuer set of the map FF. In fact, we shall prove

Theorem 2.

A non-zero constant Jacobian polynomial map F=(P,Q)F=(P,Q) has a polynomial inverse if PP is a simple polynomial.

In any meaning, the addition condition on the simple polynomial component in a non-zero constant Jacobian polynomial map may be viewed as a kind of “good” local conditions at infinity, but it seems to be not a global one. A completed classification of all simple rational polynomials was presented in [11].

2. Given a polynomial map F=(P,Q)F=(P,Q) of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}. Following [6], the non-proper value set AFA_{F} of FF is the set of all values a∈ℂ2a\in\mathbb{C}^{2} such that there exists a sequence ℂ2∋bi→∞\mathbb{C}^{2}\ni b_{i}\rightarrow\infty with F⁡(bi)→aF(b_{i})\rightarrow a. This set AFA_{F} is either empty or an algebraic curve in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} for which every irreducible component is the image of a non-constant polynomial map from ℂ\mathbb{C} into ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}. Our argument in the proof of Theorem 2 here is based on the following facts, that was presented in [13] and can be reduced from [3] (see also [14] and [15] for other refine versions).

Theorem 3.

Support F=(P,Q)F=(P,Q) is a polynomial map with non-zero constant Jacobian. If AF≠∅A_{F}\neq\emptyset, then every irreducible components of AfA_{f} can be parameterized by polynomial maps ξ↦(φ⁡(ξ),ψ⁡(ξ))\xi\mapsto(\varphi(\xi),\psi(\xi)) with

deg⁡φ/deg⁡ψ=deg⁡P/deg⁡Q.\deg\varphi/\deg\psi=\deg P/\deg Q. (1)

This theorem together with the Abhyankar-Moh Theorem [1] on the embeddings of the line to the plane allows us to obtain:

Theorem 4.

A polynomial map FF of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} must have singularities if its non-proper value set AFA_{F} has an irreducible component isomorphic to the line.

A simple proof of Theorem 4 recently presented in [15] gives a description in terms of Newton-Puiseux data how the singularity occurs in this situation.

3. To use Theorem 4 in the situation of simple polynomials, at first, we need to describe the the non-proper value curve AFA_{F} in terms of the regular extension of FF in a convenience compatification X⊃ℂ2X\supset\mathbb{C}^{2}. Given a polynomial F=(P,Q)F=(P,Q), extend it to a map F:ℙ2⟶ℙ1×ℙ1F:\mathbb{P}^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1} and resolve the points of indeterminacy to get a regular map f=(p,q):X⟶ℙ1×ℙ1f=(p,q):X\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}that coincides with F=(P,Q)F=(P,Q) on ℂ2⊂X\mathbb{C}^{2}\subset X. We call D=X−ℂ2D=X-\mathbb{C}^{2} the divisor at infinity. The divisor DD consists of a connected union of rational curves isomorphism to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} and the dual graph of the divisor DD is a tree. An irreducible component ℓ\ell of DD is a horizontal curve of PP (or QQ) if the restriction of pp (res. qq) to EE is not a constant mapping. An irreducible component ℓ\ell of DD is a dicritical curve of FF if the restriction of ff to ℓ\ell is not a constant mapping. A dicritical curve of FF must be a horizontal curve of PP or QQ. Although the compactification defined above is not unique, the horizontal curves of PP or QQ as well as the dicritical curves of FF are essentially independent of choice. Further, by blow-down components of self-intersection −1-1 corresponding to linear vertexes or endpoint in the dual graph of DD, but not of dicritical curves of FF, horizontal curves of PP or QQ, we can work with minimal compactification X⊃ℂ2X\supset\mathbb{C}^{2} on which FF can be extended to a regular morphism f=(p,q):X⟶ℙ1×ℙ1f=(p,q):X\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}.

Let us denote D∞:=f−1​(({∞}×ℙ1)∪(ℙ1×{∞}))D_{\infty}:=f^{-1}((\{\infty\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1})\cup(\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{\infty\})). The following description of the dual graph of the divisor DD is well-known (see, for example, in [18], [16] and [9]).

Proposition 1.

i) The dual graph of the divisor DD is a tree;

ii) The dual graph of the curve D∞D_{\infty} is a tree;

iii) The dual graph of each connected component of the closure of (D−D∞)(D-D_{\infty}) is a linear path of the form

⊙→∘→∘→⋯∘→∘\odot\rightarrow\circ\rightarrow\circ\rightarrow\dots\circ\rightarrow\circ

in which the beginning vertex ⊙\odot is a dicritical curve of FF and the next possible vertexes ∘\circ are curves to which the restriction of ff are finite constant mappings.

The following provides a description of the non-proper value set AFA_{F} of FF in terms of regular extension of FF in a minimal compatification X⊃ℂ2X\supset\mathbb{C}^{2}.

Proposition 2.

i)

AF=⋃dicritical curves ℓ of Ff(ℓ)∩ℂ2.A_{F}=\bigcup_{\mbox{dicritical curves }\ell\mbox{ of }F}f(\ell)\cap\mathbb{C}^{2}. (2)

ii) Let ℓ\ell be a dicritical curve of FF. Then, ℓ\ell and the curve D∞D_{\infty} have an unique common point. Let ℓ∗:=ℓ−D∞\ell^{*}:=\ell-D_{\infty}. Then, the curve ℓ∗\ell^{*} is isomorphic to ℂ\mathbb{C} and

f⁡(ℓ∗)=f⁡(ℓ)∩ℂ2f(\ell^{*})=f(\ell)\cap\mathbb{C}^{2} (3)

iii)

AF=⋃dicritical curves ℓ of Ff(ℓ∗).A_{F}=\bigcup_{\mbox{dicritical curves }\ell\mbox{ of }F}f(\ell^{*}). (4)
Proof.

Conclusion (i) can be easy verified by the definition of AFA_{F} and a simple topological argument. Conclusion (ii) follows from the fact in Proposition 1 that the dual graph of the divisor DD is a tree. Conclusion (iii) results from (i) and (ii). ∎

4. Now, we consider the situation when the restriction of pp to a dicritical curve ℓ\ell of FF is of degree 11.

Lemma 1.

Let ℓ\ell be a dicritical component of FF. If the restriction of pp to ℓ\ell is of degree 11, then the image f⁡(ℓ∗)f(\ell^{*}) is isomorphic to the line ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Proof.

Suppose ℓ\ell is a dicritical component of FF and the degree of the restriction p|ℓp_{|\ell} equals 11. Then, p|ℓ:ℓ⟶ℙ1p_{|\ell}:\ell\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} is injective, and hence, is bijective, since ℓ\ell is isomorphic to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. This ensures that the curve f⁡(ℓ∗)f(\ell^{*}) intersects each line {(u,v)∈ℂ2:u=c}\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{C}^{2}:u=c\}, c∈ℂc\in\mathbb{C}, at an unique point. Then, the polynomial H⁡(u,v)H(u,v) defining the curve f⁡(ℓ∗)⊂ℂ2f(\ell^{*})\subset\mathbb{C}^{2} can be chosen of the form v+h⁡(u)v+h(u), h∈ℂ⁡[u]h\in\mathbb{C}[u]. So, the automorphism A⁡(u,v):=(u,v−h⁡(u))A(u,v):=(u,v-h(u)) maps isomorphically the curve f⁡(ℓ∗)f(\ell^{*}) onto the line v=0v=0. ∎

Proof of Theorem 2. Suppose F=(P,Q)F=(P,Q) with J​F≡c≠0JF\equiv c\neq 0 and PP is a simple polynomial. Note that each dicritical curve of FF must be a horizontal curve of PP or QQ. Since J​F≡c≠0JF\equiv c\neq 0 and PP is simple, in view of Theorem 4 and Lemma 1, a horizontal curve of PP cannot be a dicritical curve of FF. So, if ℓ\ell is a dicritical curve of FF, then ℓ\ell must be a horizontal curve of QQ and the restriction p|ℓp_{|\ell} maps ℓ\ell to a finite constant. Thus, for such ℓ\ell the image f⁡(ℓ∗)f(\ell^{*}) is a line u=c​o​n​s​t.u=const.. The last is impossible again by Theorem 4 as J​F≡c≠0JF\equiv c\neq 0. Hence, FF has not any dicritical component. Then, AF=∅A_{F}=\emptyset by Proposition 2 and FF is a proper map by the definition of AFA_{F}. Therefore, by simple connectedness of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} the local diffeomorphic map FF must be bijective. Thus, FF is an automorphism of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}.
